set.acceptance_criteria: A session that runs worklog add and then commits the log can stop without being blocked, proven by a test in tests/test_classifier.py that commits the todo.jsonl change before running the hook. The existing controls still pass: a session that recorded nothing anywhere is still blocked, and a stale marker from a previous session does not silence a genuinely unrecorded session. hooks/stop-worklog-check.sh and plugin/hooks/scripts/stop-worklog-check.sh stay byte-identical per tests/test_plugin.py.
set.body:
The Stop hook, hooks/stop-worklog-check.sh, treats an UNCOMMITTED change to
.work/todo.jsonl as its only proof that the session recorded its work. It runs
"git diff --quiet HEAD -- .work/todo.jsonl". A session that records its items
and then commits them leaves no diff against HEAD, so the hook reads a
correctly-logged session as an unrecorded one and blocks.

This is not the worktree bug fixed earlier. Widening the search to every linked
worktree does not help, because the committed log looks identical to a log that
was never written in every checkout. The gap is equally present in a single
checkout: record, commit, keep working, and the hook blocks on the next stop.

It bites the normal working rhythm hardest. Policy says record work first, then
do it, then commit. Any session that commits mid-flight and then touches another
file walks straight into a false block. The only ways out today are to stop
committing until the turn ends, or to answer the block with prose each time.

Proposed fix: give the hook a fixed point that does not move when the session
commits. SessionStart writes the HEAD sha to a session-scoped marker file. Stop
diffs .work/todo.jsonl against that recorded sha instead of against HEAD, so
events committed during the session still count as recorded. Keep the current
HEAD diff as the fallback when no marker exists, so a session that starts
without the SessionStart hook behaves exactly as it does now.

Check the interaction with the worktree walk already in the hook: the marker is
per session, the walk is per checkout, and the fix must not let a stale marker
from an old session silence a genuinely unrecorded one.
set.title: Stop hook cannot see work that was recorded and then committed

set.acceptance_criteria: Knowledge-tree writes fail-closed without --author or SECOND_BRAIN_IDENTITY, stamp author, and emit a WriteEvent. Worklog --actor still defaults to $USER. Version 0.24.1.
set.body: Isolation says where concurrent sessions write. Identity says who wrote. Knowledge-tree writes (TicketLink and work-item nodes) must fail-closed without a claimed author and emit a WriteEvent. Worklog appends stay union-merge and keep defaulting to the local user so everyday CLI use does not break.
set.title: Wave C: require identity on knowledge-tree writes

set.acceptance_criteria: A commit pushed to main by the scheduled worklog-compact job triggers the worklog-invariants workflow, and a red result is visible on main's check history. Proven by dispatching the compact job manually and observing an invariants run attached to the commit it pushes. A deliberately broken artifact committed by that job turns the run red rather than passing silently.
set.body:
GitHub does not trigger workflows for pushes made with the default
GITHUB_TOKEN. The scheduled worklog-compact job pushes straight to main with
that token, so worklog-invariants never runs on the commits it creates.

This is how a broken main went unnoticed. The nightly job committed a log
whose provenance sha no longer matched the IA manifest. Main failed
tests/test_provenance.py on a clean checkout for two days, and the only red
signal that would have caught it never ran. It surfaced because a developer
happened to run the suite by hand.

The bug that caused that specific break is fixed. This item is about the
missing signal, which is the more expensive half: any future direct-to-main
bot commit can break the build the same silent way, and compaction is not the
only job that could gain push access.

Options, cheapest first:
  1. Have the compact job run the invariant checks itself before it pushes --
     hooks/pre-commit plus the test suite. Cheap and self-contained, but it
     duplicates the gate rather than restoring the signal, and the check
     history on main still shows nothing.
  2. Have the compact job call workflow_dispatch on worklog-invariants after
     pushing. Restores a visible run, needs the workflow to accept a ref
     input so the run attaches to the right commit.
  3. Push with a PAT or a GitHub App token instead of GITHUB_TOKEN. Triggers
     everything normally with no workflow changes, at the cost of managing a
     credential with write access to main.

Pick one deliberately. Option 1 is the smallest diff but leaves main's check
history claiming a coverage it does not have, which is its own trap.
set.title: Bot pushes to main skip CI, so a broken main goes unnoticed

set.acceptance_criteria: Running 'worklog sync --push-only --keys <one-ulid>' modifies exactly one ticket. Proven by a test that seeds two items whose local state diverges from their live tickets, syncs with --keys naming only the first, and asserts the second ticket is byte-identical afterwards -- title, status, and labels. The dry-run report lists only in-scope items, so what it previews matches what a real run does.
set.body:
'worklog sync --push-only --keys <ulid>' pushed changes to a ticket that was
not among the named keys.

Observed on 2026-08-18. The command named one key. Its log write was correctly
scoped: .work/todo.jsonl gained a single link event, for the named item only.
But the remote write was not scoped. GitHub issue 356, belonging to a different
item, had its title rewritten in the same run, confirmed by its updated
timestamp moving to the moment of the call.

The run also reported it would flip that issue from done to in_progress. That
part did not land -- the issue is still closed -- so the observed damage is a
title rewrite. Whether the status write was skipped deliberately or failed
quietly is unknown and worth finding out, because a scoped sync that silently
reopens someone's closed ticket is the more expensive version of this bug.

--keys reads as the safe way to sync one item without touching a busy log. It
is currently the opposite: it gives the false impression of a narrow blast
radius while writing as widely as an unscoped run. A reviewer approving a
one-item sync has no way to see that from the command.

The scoping needs to move to whatever builds the push set, so that both the log
writes and the remote writes derive from the same filtered list. Check whether
the same leak affects --pull-only and the drift report.
set.title: sync --keys writes to tickets outside the named scope

set.acceptance_criteria: A documented way to push a chosen set of items and nothing else. Proven by a test that seeds two items, both dirty against their live tickets, restricts the run to the first, and asserts the second ticket is untouched -- title, status, labels. The dry-run preview matches what the real run does. Existing --keys behavior is unchanged for callers who want it.
set.body:
CORRECTION. This item was filed as a P1 bug claiming that 'sync --push-only
--keys <ulid>' leaked writes to a ticket outside the named scope. That claim is
wrong. The tool did exactly what it documents.

--keys is additive, not restrictive. Its help text says "force into scope" and
the push scope is open, union hash-dirty, union --keys. Issue 356 was pushed
because it was hash-dirty, meaning its local canonical hash no longer matched
what was last synced. It was in scope with or without the flag. The proof was
already on screen: the unscoped dry run listed that same ticket before --keys
was ever passed.

What remains is a real but much smaller gap, refiled here as a feature.

There is no way to push one item and nothing else. --keys reads like a filter
to anyone who has not read the scope rule, and reaching for it to narrow a run
is the natural mistake. That is what happened: a dry run warned that a busy
ticket would be overwritten, and the obvious-looking remedy widened the run
instead of narrowing it. The dry-run preview is honest and does show this, so
the cost is a misread, not silent damage.

Two ways to close the gap. A restrictive flag, separate from --keys, that
replaces the scope rather than adding to it. Or documentation and a clearer
flag name, if the scope rule is meant to be non-negotiable and no caller should
ever push a partial set. The second is legitimate -- a sync that skips dirty
items leaves the tracker further from the log, which is the thing sync exists
to prevent.

Priority is low because nothing is broken and the dry run already shows the
truth before anything is written.
set.title: No way to restrict a sync to specific items -- --keys widens scope, it cannot narrow it

set.body: Cut v0.24.3: the four-issue fix wave (Stop hook committed-log marker, compact job self-verification, --keys documentation, Wave C item drift). Also repairs the version lockstep, which 0.24.2 left split across five sources. Released with 50 pre-existing trace-check gaps across 29 items, reported and accepted rather than skipped silently.
set.title: Release v0.24.3
